children: , the pharmaceutical and oncology heavyweight, entered the next era of commercial space research with something unusually concrete: a medicine already benefiting from work conducted in orbit. Shares rose approximately 1.0% to $146.39 Thursday, based on the latest market price.

Research aboard the International Space Station helped scientists better understand protein crystallization, contributing to the development of a faster subcutaneous formulation of blockbuster cancer drug Keytruda. NASA's research overview explains that microgravity can produce larger and more orderly protein crystals, potentially giving researchers clearer structural information. As the ISS approaches retirement, commercial stations could offer drugmakers dedicated equipment and more predictable research schedules, although regulators still lack a purpose-built approval framework for medicines manufactured in space.

The commercial stakes are already enormous. Keytruda generated about $8.37 billion of Merck's latest $16.61 billion quarter, roughly half of total revenue, while the subcutaneous version contributed $463 million, or around 5.5% of Keytruda sales. The valuation picture adds another wrinkle: at $146.39, Merck trades 21.85% above its GF Value estimate of $120.14, signaling that investors are already paying a meaningful premium to the model's estimate of fair value. Space-based research has moved beyond scientific curiosity for Merck; the harder question is whether future orbital breakthroughs can become commercially meaningful medicines often enough to justify the cost, complexity and regulatory uncertainty.

title: Merck Gains as Keytruda's Space Research Seeks a New Home
